items.prompt: What part of the eye focuses light onto the back of the eye?

options.label: The pupil
options.feedback: The pupil is just the opening that lets light in; it does not bend the light. The focusing is done by the lens.

options.label: The lens
options.feedback: Correct. The lens is a clear, curved structure that bends light rays so they meet sharply on the retina at the back of the eye.

options.label: The iris
options.feedback: The iris is the coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil. It does not focus light.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: The retina is the light-sensitive lining at the back of the eye where the image forms; it does not focus the light.

items.ok_line: The lens bends light to a sharp point on the retina.
items.ko_line: Remember: the lens, not the pupil or iris, does the focusing.
items.exp_text: The lens is a transparent, curved structure lying behind the pupil. It refracts incoming light and brings it to a sharp focus on the retina. Without it, the image would be blurry.

items.prompt: Which part of the eye is sensitive to light and sends signals to the brain?

options.label: The cornea
options.feedback: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye; it helps focus light but does not detect it. The retina does the detecting.

options.label: The sclera
options.feedback: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eye; it gives shape and protection, and it is not light-sensitive.

options.label: The vitreous humour
options.feedback: The vitreous humour is the clear jelly filling the eyeball; it holds the eye's shape but has no light-detecting cells.

options.label: The retina
options.feedback: Correct. The retina is the layer at the back of the eye packed with light-sensitive cells, rods and cones, that turn light into nerve signals.

items.ok_line: The retina turns light into signals for the brain.
items.ko_line: The retina, not the cornea or sclera, is the light-sensitive layer.
items.exp_text: The retina is a thin, light-sensitive sheet at the back of the eye. It contains millions of photoreceptor cells that convert light energy into electrical impulses, which travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

items.prompt: What shape does the pupil change to when the light is very bright?

options.label: It becomes smaller
options.feedback: Correct. In bright light the circular muscles of the iris tighten, making the pupil smaller so less light enters the eye and protects the retina from damage.

options.label: It becomes larger
options.feedback: That happens in dim light, not bright light. The pupil widens to let in more light when it is dark.

options.label: It becomes a narrow slit
options.feedback: Some animals like cats have slit pupils, but in humans the pupil stays round. In bright light it simply gets smaller as a circle.

options.label: It changes colour
options.feedback: The colour of the iris, not the size of the pupil, may look different in different lighting, but the pupil itself only changes size, not colour.

items.ok_line: Bright light makes the pupil smaller, letting in less.
items.ko_line: Bright light shrinks the pupil, not enlarges it.
items.exp_text: The pupil is the dark opening in the centre of the iris. In bright light, the iris's circular muscles contract, narrowing the pupil. This limits the amount of light entering the eye and prevents overexposure of the retina.

items.prompt: What happens to the pupil in dim light?

options.label: It stays the same size
options.feedback: It does not. The pupil changes size automatically. In dim light it widens to gather more light; it does not stay fixed.

options.label: It closes completely
options.feedback: No, closing completely would let in no light at all. Instead the pupil widens to let in as much dim light as possible.

options.label: It becomes larger
options.feedback: Correct. In dim light the iris's radial muscles relax, and the pupil widens, allowing more light to reach the retina so you can see better.

options.label: It moves to the side
options.feedback: The pupil does not move; it stays centred in the iris. Only its size changes with light level.

items.ok_line: Dim light makes the pupil larger to catch more light.
items.ko_line: In poor light the pupil opens wider, not stays or closes.
items.exp_text: When light is scarce, the radial muscles of the iris pull the pupil open wide. This enlarges the opening so more of the faint light can enter and hit the retina, improving night vision.

items.prompt: Which cells in the retina let you see colours?

options.label: Rods
options.feedback: Rods are for seeing in dim light and only in shades of grey. They do not detect colour. The colour detectors are the cones.

options.label: Ganglion cells
options.feedback: Ganglion cells carry signals from the retina to the brain; they are not the light-sensitive cells that detect colour.

options.label: Bipolar cells
options.feedback: Bipolar cells pass signals from rods and cones to ganglion cells; they do not themselves sense colour.

options.label: Cones
options.feedback: Correct. Cone cells contain three types of pigments sensitive to red, green and blue light, and their combined signals produce your full colour vision.

items.ok_line: Cone cells give you colour vision.
items.ko_line: It is the cones, not the rods, that see colours.
items.exp_text: The retina has two kinds of photoreceptors: rods and cones. Cones work best in bright light and contain pigments that respond to red, green or blue wavelengths. By comparing their signals, the brain creates the impression of colour.

items.prompt: Which cells in the retina work best in dim light and see only in shades of grey?

options.label: Cones
options.feedback: Cones need bright light to work and give colour vision. In dim light they are almost inactive. The cells that work in the dark are rods.

options.label: Rods
options.feedback: Correct. Rods are extremely sensitive to low light levels, but they contain only one pigment, so they cannot distinguish colours—only brightness.

options.label: Optic nerve fibres
options.feedback: The optic nerve carries signals to the brain; it is not a light-sensitive cell and does not work in dim light specially.

options.label: Ciliary muscles
options.feedback: These muscles change the shape of the lens to focus; they have nothing to do with detecting low light.

items.ok_line: Rods let you see in dim light, but without colour.
items.ko_line: Rods, not cones, handle dim-light vision.
items.exp_text: Rod cells are long and thin, packed with a pigment called rhodopsin that is very sensitive to low light. They fire strongly in dim conditions, but because they all have the same pigment, they only report brightness, not colour.

items.prompt: What does the hormone melatonin do to the body?

options.label: It makes you feel sleepy
options.feedback: Correct. Melatonin rises in the evening when light fades and signals the brain that it is time to sleep, lowering alertness and preparing the body for rest.

options.label: It makes you feel hungry
options.feedback: Hunger is mainly controlled by hormones like ghrelin and insulin. Melatonin is about sleep, not appetite.

options.label: It makes your skin tan
options.feedback: Tanning is caused by melanin produced in the skin when it is hit by UV light. Melatonin comes from the pineal gland and regulates sleep.

options.label: It makes your pupils larger
options.feedback: Pupil size is controlled by muscles in the iris, not by melatonin. Melatonin's main job is sleepiness.

items.ok_line: Melatonin makes the body drowsy at night.
items.ko_line: Melatonin triggers sleepiness, not hunger or tanning.
items.exp_text: Melatonin is a hormone released by the pineal gland in the brain when light levels drop. Its concentration rises through the evening and peaks in the middle of the night, promoting a state of drowsiness that helps you fall asleep and stay asleep.

items.prompt: What tells your brain's internal clock that it is time to wake up in the morning?

options.label: The stomach being empty
options.feedback: An empty stomach triggers hunger, not waking. The main signal to wake up is light entering the eyes.

options.label: The body becoming cold
options.feedback: Body temperature does change with the day, but it is not the trigger to wake. Light is the primary external signal.

options.label: Light entering the eyes
options.feedback: Correct. Light detected by special cells in the retina sends a signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock, which then suppresses melatonin and raises alertness.

options.label: The sound of your alarm
options.feedback: An alarm is a learned cue, not a natural biological signal. The body's own wake-up clock relies on light and darkness.

items.ok_line: Morning light resets the brain's internal clock.
items.ko_line: Light, not hunger or cold, tells the clock to wake.
items.exp_text: The body's internal clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain, receives a direct signal from light-sensitive cells in the retina. When morning light arrives, it suppresses melatonin and activates wake-promoting circuits, shifting your body into day mode.

items.prompt: Where is the body's main internal clock located?

options.label: In the heart
options.feedback: The heart has its own rhythm for beating, but the master clock that coordinates daily rhythms is in the brain, not the heart.

options.label: In the skin
options.feedback: Skin responds to light and vitamin D, but it does not contain the central timekeeper. That sits in the brain.

options.label: In the stomach
options.feedback: The stomach has digestive rhythms, but the overall daily clock that controls sleep, hormones and body temperature is in the brain.

options.label: In the brain
options.feedback: Correct. The suprachiasmatic nucleus, a tiny pair of nuclei in the hypothalamus, acts as the master clock, coordinating daily cycles of sleep, temperature and hormone release.

items.ok_line: The master clock sits in the brain's hypothalamus.
items.ko_line: The internal clock is in the brain, not elsewhere.
items.exp_text: The body's main circadian clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), located in the hypothalamus of the brain. It receives light signals from the eyes and synchronises the body's daily rhythms—sleep, wakefulness, temperature and hormones—to the day–night cycle.

items.prompt: What makes the skin produce more melanin?

options.label: Eating colourful food
options.feedback: Food does not make the skin produce melanin. Only sunlight (ultraviolet light) triggers the melanin-making cells.

options.label: Exposure to sunlight
options.feedback: Correct. Ultraviolet radiation in sunlight damages skin cells, and the skin responds by producing more melanin—a dark pigment that absorbs and blocks the UV rays.

options.label: Drinking more water
options.feedback: Water affects skin hydration but not melanin production. Melanin is a response to UV light, not to fluid intake.

options.label: Getting enough sleep
options.feedback: Sleep is good for the body, but it does not directly trigger melanin. Sunlight is the trigger.

items.ok_line: Sun makes the skin darken by adding melanin.
items.ko_line: Melanin comes from sunlight, not food or water.
items.exp_text: Melanin is a dark pigment produced by cells called melanocytes in the skin's outer layer. When UV light strikes the skin, it causes chemical changes that stimulate these cells to produce more melanin, which then absorbs UV rays and protects deeper cells from damage. This is why skin darkens after sun exposure.
